turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll just do your observations before the doctor calls you. Have a seat here.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Sister. Thank you very much.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): How are you feeling, in a general way?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A little tight in the chest, if I am honest, but I am coping.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Alright. Blood pressure, pulse, oxygen, then a peak flow. Sleeve up for me, please.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-six. Pulse is ninety-two. Your oxygen saturation is ninety-six percent on room air.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that within a normal range, Sister?
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor will interpret it with you. Temperature is thirty-six point seven. Now the peak flow. Big breath in, lips sealed, and blast it out hard.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do my best.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): First one is three hundred and ten. Shake it and go again.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Three hundred and forty. One last blow, please.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Three hundred and fifty. Best of three is three hundred and fifty litres per minute. I'll write that down. Doctor Naidoo will be with you just now.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Sister. I appreciate it.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Doctor Naidoo. Sorry about the wait. Tell me what's been going on.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I have been wheezing since a cold last week, and it has not properly settled.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): A cold, and then the wheeze stayed. How has it felt for you day to day?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The cold was mostly a runny nose and a sore throat, and those have gone. What is left is a dry cough, and a whistle when I breathe, particularly on the stairs up to the flat.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's miserable on the stairs. When you say last week, can you place the first day at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not entirely sure. It was sometime early last week. Perhaps Monday, perhaps Tuesday. I cannot be precise, I am afraid.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can work with that. Any fever now?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I have not felt feverish at all.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And any pain in the chest?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. There is no chest pain.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you bringing anything up with the cough?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stays dry. Nothing comes up.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you wake at night with the wheezing?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. It is difficult to say.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. We'll leave that one a bit open. Have you got inhalers at home?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. A blue one and a brown one. I must admit I confuse the two.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not the first, don't worry. Which one do you grab when the chest gets tight?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I had thought the brown one was the quick-relief inhaler. My cousin then said, no, the blue one is the reliever. I may have used the wrong one for a day or two.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's read the labels. What does the blue one say?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): It says salbutamol, one hundred micrograms. I think the brand is Ventolin. I take two puffs.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the brown one?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Beclomethasone. I believe it is two hundred micrograms, though the chemist label has faded somewhat.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): And how often are you actually using that blue salbutamol at the moment?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe five, six times a day. I am not counting it properly. I use it whenever the whistle starts.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about the brown one, the beclomethasone preventer, every morning and every evening as it was meant to be?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I forget it when I am rushing to lectures.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the preventer is hit and miss. Were you ever on anything else for the asthma?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to take montelukast, ten milligrams at night. I stopped it in March. It gave me rather odd dreams.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March, thank you. Was anything else prescribed that you never actually started?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): The clinic wrote amoxicillin last week, for the cold. Five hundred milligrams three times a day. I never took it. I did not feel it was warranted.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we won't count that as a medicine you're on. Anything from the chemist, even for the nose?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I take loratadine, ten milligrams, by mouth, if my nose is itchy. I have been taking it daily since the cold.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines that you know of?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Penicillin has always been perfectly fine. I simply chose not to use the amoxicillin.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does asthma run in the family at all?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother has asthma. She still uses an inhaler daily.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): And smoking?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have never smoked. I do not drink a great deal either. Perhaps a beer at the weekend, not every week.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you busy with these days, work or studies?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I am in second year, accounting, at UJ. I share a flat in Auckland Park with two friends. The stairs are the difficulty at present.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Load shedding has made this winter feel longer, hasn't it. Has the cough kept you out of lectures?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I missed one lecture on Thursday, but that was the traffic, a robot that was out near campus, not really the cough. I am still attending.

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Let me have a listen. Deep breaths in... There is a scattered wheeze on both sides, a little more on the right. No crackles. Your throat looks clear, and you are not pulling in at the neck.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. Is that a serious finding, Doctor?

[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think this is your asthma flaring after the cold, not a pneumonia. The peak flow Sister recorded, best of three hundred and fifty, is a bit down if your usual sits around five hundred, but you are speaking in full sentences and your oxygen is ninety-six.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): When I last had it checked at the campus clinic, it was about four hundred and eighty. That was some months ago, though.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that helps. I would like to add a short steroid course to settle this. Prednisone, forty milligrams each morning, for five days, by mouth. Take it with food.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty milligrams, for five days. Yes, I understand.

[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the blue salbutamol, two puffs when you need it, but if you are still on it maybe five or six times a day after a couple of days, that is too often and I want to hear about it. The brown beclomethasone, two hundred micrograms, two puffs in the morning and two puffs in the evening, every day, even on good days. Rinse your mouth afterwards.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall be more careful with the brown inhaler. I had the colours the wrong way round.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): We might do a chest X-ray if this does not settle. I do not think you need one today.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): I would prefer to avoid the X-ray if it is not required.

[SEG0069] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks. Sooner, of course, if the breathing gets worse, if you cannot finish a sentence, or if the salbutamol stops helping. Reception can book that two-week visit.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I develop a fever, should I come earlier?
[SEG0071] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. If you spike a fever, or you start coughing up coloured phlegm, come back before the two weeks. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Is there anything further I ought to watch for?

[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rest, drink fluids, and finish the five days of prednisone even if you feel better by day three. Don't start that amoxicillin. Bring both inhalers next time so we can check your technique.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): I will bring them both. Thank you for clarifying the colours.
[SEG0075] person_3 (DOCTOR): Easy thing to mix up. You did the right thing coming in. See you in two weeks, and I hope those stairs feel kinder.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Goodbye, Doctor. And please thank Sister for her kindness as well.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Peak flow completed by nurse supported; indication 'wheeze after a cold' not stated by nurse.
bad.text: peak expiratory flow (type=other, status=completed, requested_by=nurse, indication=wheeze after a cold)

omissions.text: Night waking with wheeze was asked about and the answer was equivocal/uncertain: 'Sometimes, not really. It is difficult to say.'

The patient had confused the inhaler roles and may have used the wrong inhaler for a day or two; they thought the brown inhaler was the quick-relief inhaler before being corrected that the blue inhaler is the reliever.
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day was prescribed by the clinic last week for the cold but was never started; this should be recorded as not taken rather than omitted as merely 'not on'.
The patient reports penicillin has always been perfectly fine, clarifying no penicillin allergy despite declining amoxicillin.
Doctor noted the patient was speaking in full sentences.
Usual/recent baseline peak flow was about 480 L/min at the campus clinic some months ago; doctor referenced usual around 500 and patient clarified about 480.
